#106220. Arsenal 1-1 Dortmund: Familiar flaws hold Arsenal back

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1704 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arseblog ↗ Open Full Page

Arsenal 1-1 Dortmund: Familiar flaws hold Arsenal back

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday raised some very familiar concerns and, if we’re being honest, revealed nothing we didn’t already know.
  • Arsenal can play world-class football and completely dominate teams for long spells, but lack the world-class attack to make the most of that domination, the sort of players you just know will create and convert significant chances when the time comes.
  • I really feel like I could write two versions of today’s blog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday raised some very familiar concerns and, if we’re being honest, revealed nothing we didn’t already know.

Arsenal can play world-class football and completely dominate teams for long spells, but lack the world-class attack to make the most of that domination, the sort of players you just know will create and convert significant chances when the time comes. And the way the team is starting games after the break is worrying, with teams who are battered to within an inch of their lives early on suddenly able to compete.

I really feel like I could write two versions of today’s blog. One where I’m miserable, of course: the players can’t shoot, they make all the wrong choices in the decisive moment, we can’t keep wasting chances and dropping off after the break, if Andrea Berta doesn’t deliver the true heirs to Thierry Henry and Robert Pires in January, then he should be stuffed into one of the cannons outside the Armoury and fired into the cold night air.

The other version is much more glass half full: Arteta is coaching masterclasses every week, this level of dominance in games is something I could only dream of a few years ago, that’s the most shots we’ve had in a game all season, we’re top of the league, we’re creating loads without any set-piece reliance and without Bukayo Saka – the goals will come.

Industry observers note that some people reading this would prefer (and relate better to) one version, and others the other version, I’m sure. Let’s see where we end up!

It has been revealed that there were, as there tends to be in these Champions League games, a fair few changes from the weekend. Kepa, Piero Hincapie, Ben White, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Christos Tzolis, and Viktor Gyokeres all came into the team.

Despite featuring half a different side, there were plenty of parallels with the Newcastle match. Arsenal were dominant from the off, with Hincapie and White taking turns to play off of Gyokeres. Dortmund had no idea how to cover them and both fullbacks were the targets of early crosses into the box.

After a couple of long-range efforts, Arsenal got their goal they deserved, with Gyokeres launching a ferocious, dipping effort beyond Gregor Kobel. The Swede can put his foot through the ball, that’s for sure, and the Dortmund backline gave him the sort of time and space to set himself that he doesn’t often get.

The pressure continued after the opener for a while, with Tzolis forcing a good save and Madueke just unable to sort his feet to tap in the rebound.

It’s fair to say the game settled down after 15/20 minutes, with Dortmund growing into it a little, but it was still Arsenal who looked like scoring the next goal. Rice shot over from almost the same patch of grass Gyokeres had scored from, and the midfielder had another chance when a beautiful one-touch move ended with him bursting through, hurtling towards the Dortmund box. Maybe he could’ve picked out Madueke in support, but he went alone and Nico Schlotterbeck just got across to block the shot.

In a recent development, another huge chance was denied by the offside flag as much as the finishing – Madueke won the ball high, Odegaard squared it to Gyokeres, and the Swede fired over from near the penalty spot. Odegaard was ruled offside but I’m not convinced: had the ball hit the net, I think we’d have seen a very tight VAR check.

In a recent development, there was one thought on everyone’s minds at half-time: don’t do the same thing again. After Slavia Prague and Newcastle, do not do the same thing again.

Arsenal did the same thing again.

There was an early warning sign with Dortmund sliding the ball across the box and Maximilian Beier kicking the air. He didn’t make the same mistake with his next opportunity. Centre-back Joane Gadou (who was very impressive all evening) charged through the heart of the pitch before playing the ball to Beier, who jinked to unbalance Gabriel and slotted home.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes a goal is just a good goal, and I don’t think anyone was really at fault here. It’s a great run from Gadou, Beier tricks Gabriel to take the ball onto his weaker left side – it’s fair if Gabriel is expecting (and blocking the angle) on the attacker’s favoured foot, I know how that can happen. I think if we score that goal we’re talking about two brilliant individuals, rather than defensive errors.

My first thought? Not again. My second? OK, how do we respond? Because on Saturday, the response was poor.

This time it was a lot better. Jobe Bellingham had a rebound disallowed for offside, a moment that really brought the crowd back into the game, but in truth, that was Dortmund’s only real moment of threat. From the goal on 55 minutes to full-time, Arsenal had 15 shots to Dortmund’s two.

And that doesn’t include Serhou Guirassy playing one-twos with the post after a clever, low free-kick from Martin Odegaard late on.

Sources indicate that madueke had an effort blocked. Gyokeres flicked a header wide. Madueke shot wide beyond the far post after a good run. Gyokeres missed a major chance with his head from six yards out. Rice hit the near post from a tight angle after a brilliant pass from Eberechi Eze.

A couple of late corners came to nothing, and that was it.

Mikel Arteta was clearly pleased with the performance on the whole:.

Sources indicate that well, I think I love the way the team played. There’s no question how superior, how dominant, how much of a threat we were, how connected everybody was to the game … It was great to watch. It was unbelievable that sometimes the ball hasn’t ended up in the back of the net. That’s my feeling.

to do what we’ve done out there is just something to be very, very pleased about, because there is very little more that we can demand from the team.

But we all know what that little more is:.

Recent findings suggest that obviously the feeling is that we should reward ourselves much more when you put that kind of performance, the amount of chances, the situation, and even shots that are not there. We are three against two, two against one, and the ball doesn’t land with the right person. There is an element of luck, there is an element of us finishing the actions better. We need to insist, because I think what the team has done and shown today is the right direction.

In a recent development, often when Arsenal don’t win games, it feels like it’s because the team haven’t created enough chances. We end up focusing on that one moment, where that one player didn’t execute the way you wanted. But last night wasn’t one of those: Arsenal didn’t struggle to turn dominance into good, slick football, and that football into a healthy number of decent opportunities.

That’s incredibly frustrating, but I do think you win a lot more often than not when you do that. Maybe that’s a hard sell for some this morning, but it’s how I feel about it when we play well, especially when we’ve been winning games anyway. That’s the first time this season we’ve gone two without a win across all competitions, and we’ve won 14 of 19 games so far. Sometimes things don’t fall for you, and this one felt a lot like ‘one of those’, certainly more than Newcastle did.

A word for a couple of promising performances too, with the boss asked about Gyokeres in his post-match press conference:.

Sources indicate that what I love the most is how connected he was to the team. We used him many times in different ways. His link-up play, the way he held the ball, the way he threw it in behind and stretched the pitch. There was a lot to like in that performance and that’s the victory that we need.

His finishing was off after the brilliant opener, but at least he was in the positions: too often this season and last, Gyokeres has gone through a game barely registering a shot. He had seven last night, and if he can do that more often he’ll score a lot more. His general play was improved too, both holding the ball up and competing in behind.

It has been revealed that and I thought Martin Odegaard was excellent too. His eight chances created from open play was the most of any player in any Champions League match so far this season.

According to recent reports, since we returned to the competition in 2023, we’ve had a player create more than five chances in a match just twice: Odegaard at Napoli in September (6) and Odegaard last night (9). He’s incredibly unlucky not to be leaving the game with a couple of assists.

The draw leaves us in a decent position to finish in the all-key top eight in the league phase still, although you have to squint a bit to see us landing in the also-important top two. Real Madrid are up next and that’s a reminder of the sort of teams we’re up against: finishing in the top two is a tall order at the best of times.

With each passing game, it is impossible not to wonder what could be done in January to add to the team. Unless there’s a sudden uptick out of nowhere, those thoughts aren’t disappearing. And even if there is a massive uptick, those thoughts will still be around. But 30 shots is the most we’ve had in a game all season, and the same group of players have scored more goals with fewer shots (/chances) plenty of times. Let’s hope we see some more clinical finishing on Sunday.

Guess I landed on the glass half full version.

Industry observers note that there should be an Arsecast once Blogs has caught up with the game, so stay tuned for that. Enjoy your Wednesdays!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool have already been linked with a lot of players this season.

The Anfield outfit seem to have many different areas of their first-team squad that need upgrading despite them spending well obver £600 million on fresh players across the last couple of years.

These transfers were expected to set the Reds up for a while but, in reality, they just highlighted other problems that Andoni Iraola has among his ranks.

They're currently fourth in the Premier League table which, while a decent result, is far away from where they need to be.

With players such as Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz among their ranks, they should be one of the best teams in the world but, instead, they just about scraping qualification for the Champions League.

This needs to change and, with the January transfer window now just around the corner, it could be about to.

Liverpool are 'keeping a close eye' on Nico Paz.

Over the last couple of years, Liverpool's attack has been their main focus of interest in the transfer market.

Mohamed Salah, Sadio Mane and Roberto Firmino have all left now and, with Iraola at the helm, a upcoming style of football has also made its way to Anfield this term.

His heavy-metal style of play has some similarities to Jurgen Klopp's and, after two season of Arne Slot, it was a welcome re-jig.

This summer alone, over £150 million was spent with the Reds' attack taking most of the money.

But, that hasn't stopped Liverpool from being linked with even more attackers.

In fact, a fresh patch from journalist Ben Fernandes Santos has just shared that the Anfield outfit are one of the many clubs who are keeping a 'close eye' on Como's Nico Paz.

"Liverpool, Arsenal and Tottenham are keeping a close eye on Nico Paz," he wrote.

"The Argentine is focused on Como, but the summer will be crucial for his future. The trend is that he won't return to Real Madrid, despite being well liked at Valdebebas.

"Arda Güler's contract renewal has been announced, and Bellingham's will come soon. Nico knows this, and it will influence his decision.

"If Real Madrid don't win any titles, they'll look to sign a creative midfielder. Mourinho is delighted with the Tchouaméni - Bernardo Silva double pivot.

"The priority remains a centre-back, with Jacobo Ramón at the top of the list.".

Nico Paz would be an unreal addition for Liverpool.

Nobody knows what Liverpool's first-team squad is going to look like in 2027.

The January transfer window is just over a month away and, with the number of players who have been linked with a switch, a huge rebuild could be on its way.

And then, in the summer, another rebuild could take place.

Paz is a highly sought-after attacker that has long been linked with a Liverpool transfer.

He's Como's best player and, the fact that he's contributed to 14 goals in the 16 games he's played this season prove how good he actually is.

Whether he's used as a number 10, a right winger or a striker, Liverpool would have an incredible player on their hands if they manage to get a deal over the line.

Here's hoping they do and the Reds add even more firepower to their already stacked attack.

Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that modern and future electronics harbour a key challenge: as conventional metal wires shrink to nanoscale dimensions, their resistivity increases sharply1 owing to surface and grain-boundary scattering.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that modern and future electronics harbour a key challenge: as conventional metal wires shrink to nanoscale dimensions, their resistivity increases sharply1 owing to surface and grain-boundary scattering. To circumvent this unwanted behaviour, here, we explore the fundamental limits of charge transport in topological semimetal niobium phosphide (NbP) nanoribbons down to approximately 6-nm widths, with industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication. The extracted NbP nanoribbon resistivity reaches 18 ± 4.1 μΩ cm at room temperature with an approximately 9-nm2 cross-sectional area, lower than that of conventional metals and semimetals with comparable size. The NbP nanoribbon resistivity decreases with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper. This trend suggests a growing relative contribution of surface and edge states as the nanoribbon cross-section is reduced, despite a certain amount of disorder, including edge roughness. Our findings advance the understanding of size-dependent transport and scaling in this class of semimetals, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects in future nanoelectronics.

Recent findings suggest that a, High-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) image of the NbP (1.5 nm) nanoribbon with Nb (3.4 nm) seed layer. The electrically-conducting width of this device is ~12.5 nm. b, Magnified view of the nanocrystalline NbP layer and crystalline Nb seed, together with their corresponding Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), obtained from the boxed regions in panel a. c,d, Bright-field image (c) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental map (d) of the same device, showing distinct material compositions. In total, three NbP (1.5 nm) nanoribbons were examined by cross-sectional STEM. Across these samples, we observe consistent structural and compositional characteristics, including similar NbP crystallinity and sidewall oxidation, which support the scaling behaviour reported in this work. Additional STEM characterization was not performed on thicker NbP nanoribbons, as the thinnest nanoribbons are most relevant to the main conclusions of this study.

Sources indicate that a, HAADF image of the NbP (1.5 nm)/Nb (3.4 nm) nanoribbon with an electrically-conducting width of ~18 nm. b, Magnified view of the nanocrystalline NbP layer and crystalline Nb seed layer, together with their corresponding FFT, obtained from the boxed regions. c,d, Bright-field image (c) and EDS elemental map (d) of the same device, showing distinct material compositions of each region. e, EELS linescan profiles of Nb (blue) and P (red) normalized intensity as a function of position along the direction indicated in panel c. f-h, Representative nanobeam electron diffraction (NBED) patterns extracted from 4D-STEM data at probe positions within the sapphire substrate (f), Nb layer (g), and NbP layer (h), with indexed reflections confirming the distinct crystal structure of each region. i-k, Orientation template matching of the representative NBED pattern in f–h, for the sapphire substrate (i), Nb layer (j) and NbP layer (k). Coloured symbols indicate the local crystallographic orientation of the best-matching template for that pattern. l-n, Phase template matching of the same patterns for the sapphire substrate (l), Nb layer (m) and NbP layer (n).

In a recent development, a, Schematic of the scaling mechanism for conventional metals, with surface scattering and grain boundary scattering. b, As thickness and width of NbP are reduced, the conduction is consistent with the growing dominance of surface carriers, which are disorder-tolerant, with reduced scattering. The total sheet conductance in this case is a sum of the sheet conductance contributed from bulk carriers and surface carriers. c, For thick NbP, bulk carriers dominate the transport, and thus conventional scaling laws apply, with pronounced surface and grain boundary scattering. d, The Fuchs-Sondheimer (FS) and Mayadas-Shatzkes (MS) model fitting of 3.4 nm Nb seed layer, showing an excellent fit. The extracted resistivity with increasing width (W → ∞) is 56.3 μΩ∙cm, which matches the literature results. e, Sheet conductance (GNbP,□) of 1.5 nm NbP as a function of width (red curve), extracted from Fig. 2d of the main text. The sheet conductance from bulk carriers (extracted from Hall measurement) follows the conventional FS-MS scaling model (black dashed line), where the sheet conductance from surface carriers increases as the width decreases due to the increased surface area/volume ratio, as indicated by the purple dashed line. At this ultrathin thickness (1.5 nm), bulk carriers experience strong scattering, resulting in very small bulk carrier sheet conductance. f, GNbP,□ of 10 nm NbP as a function of width (blue curve). At NbP thickness of 10 nm, 3D bulk carriers and 2D top and bottom surface carriers contribute comparably to transport, as shown in Fig. 4b. At this thickness, as the nanoribbon width is reduced, the enhancement in surface conduction is insufficient to offset the increased scattering of bulk carriers. Consequently, bulk transport dominates in this regime, leading to a net reduction of sheet conductance (i.e., increased resistivity) with decreasing width, more similar to conventional metal wires. We note that there could be subtle differences in sidewall roughness and damage in the thicker nanoribbons compared to the thinner ones. See Supplementary Note 2 for the modelling details and more discussion.

a, Bulk Brillouin-zone schematic showing the two mirror planes and nodal rings from the band inversion. b, Representative band dispersion along Γ-S-M’, where the curves calculated without spin-orbit coupling (SOC) show the nodal-ring-related band inversion (plotted in green), and the curves calculated with SOC show the corresponding gap opening (black dashed lines). c, Real-space crystal view highlighting the helical states along the projected mirror line on the surface. d, Surface-state spectrum along \(\overline{\Gamma }\)-\(\overline{{\rm{X}}}\)-\(\overline{\Gamma }\)’, where the narrow Weyl-point window (grey shadow) hosts three pairs of helical states (indicated by arrows) that form the main part of the Fermi arcs, while remnant spin-split surface branches remain visible over a broader energy window (broad green shadow). Blue and red colours indicate the ‘± Sy’ spin polarization at opposite momenta, showing the helical feature. In summary, the narrow Fermi-arc structure is embedded inside a much broader nodal-ring-derived surface-state sector set by the band inversion. See Supplementary Note 7 for more discussion on bulk-topology hierarchy and topological surface-state interpretation.

a, Slab model along the [001] direction for the surface state calculations. Here, the 2 × 2 × 3 supercell is shown as an example. A 4.5 nm thick slab structure of the 1 × 1 × 4 supercell was used in the calculations. b,c, Surface band structures with Nb (b) and P (c) terminations along high-symmetry lines. Blue and red bands indicate the surface states of the Nb and P terminations, respectively. Bulk-projected states shown in pale blue are depicted as the background. The charge neutral point is set to 0 eV. d-f, Surface-projected Fermi surfaces with Nb (upper panels) and P (lower panels) terminations at 0 eV (d), −0.2 eV (e), and −0.4 eV (f). Darker colours represent larger contributions projected from the surface. Weyl points projected on the 2D Brillouin zone are shown as green and purple dots for opposite chirality. The constant energy cuts show surface-dominant open contours over a broad energy window, indicating that Weyl-derived surface bands persist even when the chemical potential is shifted deep into the hole-doped regime, which implies the robustness of the topological surface character. In addition, for the 4.5 nm thick NbP film, the top and bottom surface states exhibit minimal hybridization, except near the Weyl point projections where they meet each other. The Fermi-arc states remain largely unhybridized because they are well separated in momentum space. Even at momenta where they intersect, the resulting hybridization gap is negligible. See Supplementary Note 8 for the modelling details and more discussion.

a, Slab model from the NbP (001) film with thickness d = 1.5 nm and width W = 4.4 to 5.7 nm. b, The one-dimensional (1D) band structure of a W = 5 nm nanoribbon along ky direction. The edge projection is highlighted in purple to show the edge states, while the bulk states are shown in pale blue. Near EF, the edge-projected subbands form an electron-like pocket, consistent with the negative pedge values (panel f). c-e, The spin projection to Sx (c), Sy (d), and Sz (e) components, respectively, for the edge state. The blue and red represent opposite signs of spin polarization. These edge states exhibit a pronounced spin texture arising from strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in noncentrosymmetric NbP where Sx and Sz components are locked to the ky momentum in a Rashba-type SOC. This reduces the wavefunction overlap between counter-propagating modes, thereby suppressing the leading backscattering channel, which indicates high-mobility edge conduction. f, The carrier densities from edge (pedge) and 2D film (p2D) are extracted from linear fitting of the total ribbon density (p1D) by p1D = pedge + p2DW, at varying W. Wc denotes the cross-over width at which the edge carrier density would dominate the transport over the top and bottom surface carrier density. Here, Wc ≈ 0 indicates that the enhanced edge conduction of ultrathin films is not primarily driven by an increased edge carrier density. Instead, it is more plausibly attributed to an enhanced carrier mobility arising from reduced backscattering as the edge dimension approaches the quasi-1D limit. See more details in Supplementary Notes 2 and 8. g, Agreement between the nanoribbon fitting (\({p}_{2{\rm{D}}}^{{\rm{NR}}}\)) and that obtained from independent slab film calculations (\({p}_{2{\rm{D}}}^{{\rm{slab}}}\)) which corresponds to the d = 1.5 nm thickness in Supplementary Fig. 10. This agreement supports the self-consistency of our calculations across both the nanoribbon and thin-film geometries.

According to recent reports, a, Temperature-dependent effective resistivity (ρeff) of NbP films with different thicknesses up to 90 nm, measured from Hall bar devices. These films have a 3.4 nm Nb seed layer, whose resistivity is measured separately (black symbols). b, Low-temperature limit (2-10 K) of panel a. The smallest superconducting transition temperature Tc (~2.2 K) is in the 3.4 nm Nb layer (black symbols), while higher Tc are observed in the NbP/Nb films, and Tc decreases monotonically with thicker NbP. The symbol colours follow the convention in panel a. c,d, Temperature-dependent sheet conductance (GNbP,□) (c) and resistivity (ρNbP) (d) for all NbP thicknesses, after subtracting the Nb seed contribution. e, ρNbP as a function of NbP thickness at 300 K and 10 K. For comparison, the ρNbP values of nanoribbons with the widest widths (Fig. 2d of the main text) are slightly higher than those from Hall measurements at 300 K, possibly due to process-induced damage during nanofabrication. f, Temperature-dependent ρeff of a ~5 nm-thick Nb control film, measured from a Hall bar device. The residual resistivity ratio (RRR) is 1.48, and the Tc is ~4.2 K. Inset: enlarged view of the low-temperature region. The presence of NbP appears to promote superconductivity in NbP/Nb films. The superconducting proximity effect is one plausible interpretation, although changes in disorder and enhanced inter-grain coupling (in the presence of NbP layer) could also contribute. We also cannot fully rule out the formation of an interfacial superconducting layer at the NbP/Nb interface. The NbP sheet conductance is obtained by subtracting the sheet conductance of the Nb layer (measured independently on control Nb films) from the total sheet conductance of the NbP/Nb stack. The extracted NbP resistivity is then obtained by dividing the NbP thickness by the NbP sheet conductance, i.e. ρNbP = dNbP/GNbP,□, where GNbP,□ = Gtot,□ - GNb,□ and Gtot,□ = dtot/ρeff, where Gtot,□ is the total sheet conductance of the NbP/Nb stack, dtot is the total stack thickness and ρeff is the measured effective resistivity (panel a). The GNbP,□ (panel c) represents the NbP sheet conductance after subtracting the independently-measured Nb seed contribution. Additional validation of the subtraction method using Pt/Nb stacks is provided in Supplementary Fig. 19. Control experiments using Pt/Nb stacks validate that the subtraction procedure itself does not generate an anomalous resistivity trend. Nevertheless, the conductance of the Nb seed layer within NbP/Nb stacks cannot be independently measured and it cannot be noted, with absolute certainty, that its behaviour is identical to that of the separately measured Nb control film. Thus, the extracted NbP resistivity relies, by necessity, on the model used.

It has been revealed that a-c, Hall resistance (Rxy) vs. magnetic field (B) measured at various temperatures for 3.4 nm Nb (a), 1.5 nm NbP (b), and 10 nm NbP (c). For the NbP films (b,c), the Nb seed layer contribution is subtracted at each corresponding temperature to extract NbP Hall response, using the same two-layer Hall conduction model described in the supplement. d, Effective three-dimensional carrier density (p3D) for all films, revealing opposite temperature-dependence: ultrathin 1.5 nm NbP reveals an increasing p3D upon cooling, whereas both thicker NbP (10 nm) and Nb (3.4 nm) display decreasing p3D. (This figure is also included in the main text as Fig. 4d and is reproduced here for convenience). e, Effective hole mobility (μp) of the same films vs. temperature. NbP films exhibit a pronounced increase in mobility upon cooling due to suppressed phonon scattering, whereas the 3.4 nm Nb film shows only a slight rise in mobility, indicating that its transport remains strongly limited by surface scattering.

Industry observers note that a-c, Longitudinal sheet resistance (Rxx) vs. magnetic field (B) measured at various temperatures for films of Nb seed layer (3.4 nm) (a), for NbP (1.5 nm) on the Nb seed (b), and for NbP (10 nm) on the Nb seed (c). All measurements were performed with the magnetic field applied perpendicular to the film plane and current direction. At low temperatures, all films exhibit a pronounced negative cusp near low field regions, arising from the interplay of superconducting fluctuations and weak antilocalization. d-e, Longitudinal sheet resistance (Rxx) vs. magnetic field (B) measured at 1.8 K for both 1.5 nm thick NbP (on 3.4 nm Nb seed layer) and for the Nb layer (3.4 nm) evaluated separately. Measurements were performed with B field perpendicular to the film plane and current direction (d), and with B applied in-plane (e). The superconducting transition temperatures are Tc ~ 6 K for the 1.5 nm NbP (on Nb) and ~2.2 K for the 3.4 nm Nb film (see Fig. 3d of the main text). The upper critical field Hc2, defined as the midpoint between the normal state resistance and zero resistance, is extracted. At 1.8 K, the out-of-plane critical field \({H}_{c2}^{\perp }\) is 2.2 T for NbP (1.5 nm) and 0.38 T for Nb (3.4 nm). The in-plane critical field at 1.8 K exceeds 9 T for NbP (1.5 nm) and reaches 4.44 T for Nb (3.4 nm). The superconducting coherence length estimates are provided in the supplement. The sense current used for Hall bar measurements is 0.5 mA, corresponding to a current density of ~0.1 MA/cm2 for the NbP (1.5 nm) film and ~0.15 MA/cm2 for the 3.4 nm Nb control, with the same 100 μm Hall bar device width. We note that this sense current is well below the superconducting critical current: even when we increased the sense current up to 10 mA, we were unable to suppress the superconducting state at 1.8 K.

a, Cross-sectional HAADF STEM image of the alternating NbP/Nb multilayers grown on sapphire. b-d, Denoised nanobeam electron diffraction (NBED) patterns extracted from 4D-STEM data for all Nb layers (Nb layers 1-3) showing consistent body-centred cubic (bcc) diffraction symmetry with indexed reflections, confirming crystalline quality across all Nb layers. Scale bars: 0.5 Å−1. e, EDS line scan across the multilayer stack showing Nb (blue), P (red), and Al (light brown) as a function of position, integrated over a ~ 5nm wide region along the direction indicated by the yellow arrow in panel a, confirming periodic composition and abrupt elemental transitions at each NbP/Nb interface. f-h, denoised NBED patterns from NbP layers 1–3, displaying diffraction symmetry consistent with the NbP crystal structure with indexed reflections, consistent with uniform phase and crystallographic orientation throughout the multilayer stack. The diffraction spots become progressively broader from layer 1 to layer 3, suggesting a gradual decrease in crystalline coherence in NbP layers further from the substrate. This is further supported by the emergence of diffuse ring features in the Layer 3 diffraction pattern, indicative of increasing structural disorder.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tomorrow evening, AC Milan will entrust Ardon Jashari with the job of filling Luka Modric’s shoes, after the Croatian’s injury.
  • In a recent development, if you missed last night’s reporting, Milan have been dealt a bit of a blow ahead of their game against Olympiacos, as Modric has suffered a muscle strain.
  • Nevertheless, it creates a short-term matter and in a midfield where only a few names have convinced, it plunges Ruben Amorim into the water somewhat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tomorrow evening, AC Milan will entrust Ardon Jashari with the job of filling Luka Modric’s shoes, after the Croatian’s injury.

Industry observers note that since he arrived, Jashari has been seen as the next in line for Modric, but he’s never shown performances to match that eventual rise. However, Gazzetta dello Sport (as seen below) write that he could take that step against Olympiacos.

Sources indicate that it opens a space for Jashari, but filling Modric’s boots will not be an easy task. In fact, he’ll have to be at his best to replace him, especially in a game with so much on the line.

Looking at the Europa League table, the Rossoneri need to be perfect if they’re to have any chance of a top eight finish. For him, though, Jashari must be perfect if his journey at San Siro is to continue.

So far, his time in Italy has been marred by injury and a failure to establish himself as a starter, or even a key rotational option. Yet, the Diavolo never gave up on him, refusing a sale in the summer.

Now, it is time to repay that in a game where ‘everything looks different’. For Jashari, it’s a simple task: be solid. He’s got a guaranteed place, reliable teammates around him and the trust to act.

No one can challenge him for the next five days; the spot is guaranteed. It’ll be up to him if those five days become 10 or more. If not, there’s a market waiting for him.

The 25-year-old Frenchman, one half of a defence partnership alongside Levi Colwill that has struggled this season, conducted a two-hour chat with a French YouTube channel. It is understood the interview was not arranged by Chelsea, who have lost three of their last four league fixtures and are in an uncomfortable moment under fresh manager, Xabi Alonso.

Wesley Fofana risked winding up Chelsea fans with his interview on French YouTube channel.

Fofana smashed his penalty over the bar against Liverpool in October but saw the funny side.

Previously plagued by injuries, Fofana revealed how he considered retirement until he was seemingly advised to honour his contract with Chelsea by his representative.

After taking the points on his driving licence to 50 in January of this year, his lawyer disclosed his salary in a statement to the court, revealing that his client is paid more than £200,000 per week.

He is contracted to Chelsea until 2029.

‘I really wanted to stop, because, for the first time in my life, I wasn’t happy anymore. I thought to myself, “I’m too fragile, I’m the Abou Diaby of our generation. There has to be someone like that, and it happened to me. It’s my destiny, I accept it.”.

‘Of course, I was very sad and didn’t want to stop, because I was living my dream.

Industry observers note that ‘I sat down with my agents. “I’m not going to play football anymore.” Then they told me about the contract, et cetera.

Cristiano Ronaldo took to social media on Thursday to announce that he had played his last game for Portugal.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the No. 7 shirt of our national team," the 41-year-old Ronaldo remarked in a video on his Instagram account.

"I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world," Ronaldo mentioned.

The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus forward represented his country 234 times, scoring 146 goals — making him the men's record-holder for ⁠international ​appearances and for international goals.

He captained Portugal ​to their first major trophy at ​Euro 2016 and led them to the 2019 and 2025 Nations League titles.

In a recent development, "It was not an easy decision, there are decisions that are not ​only with the head. They are also made with the heart," Ronaldo continued in the Instagram post.

"If I ever made you happy, ​if one of my goals ever made you hug someone, forget a worry or feel ⁠proud ​of our country, then it ​was all worth it.".

He also thanked his family, the Portuguese people ​and the teammates, coaches and staff he worked with over his national ​team career.

The Portuguese Football Association (FPF) released a statement expressing its gratitude and respect for the player also known as "CR7.".

"Cristiano Ronaldo has raised Portugal's profile and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps; for many of us, he is the greatest player of all time!" it read.

The FPF intends to organize a tribute "in which the fans and the country can one more time applaud and celebrate a player who has given us so much.".

In a recent development, while his long-rival Lionel Messi ended his Argentina career with a much anticipated farewell match last month, Ronaldo's final appearance may go down as Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales on September 24, depending on the nature of the tribute. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus left him on the bench for the following match and said he wouldn't start the next one.

According to recent reports, ronaldo responded by walking out of the Portugal training camp. He was subsequently suspended and fined by the FPF, but he had been expected to return to Portugal for the November international break.

Like Messi, Ronaldo intends to continue his club career with Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia.

It’s a substantial day for Alex Coles, who celebrates his milestone 150th cap today.

The 27-year-old lock follows Fraser Dingwall, Rory Hutchinson and Alex Mitchell to become the fourth member of Saints’ current squad to reach 150 appearances for his boyhood club, eight years after making his debut in 2018.

Coles marks one of nine changes to Saints’ side for the Derby Day clash, with Emmanuel Iyogun, Curtis Langdon, Ed Prowse, Tom Pearson and Henry Pollock the other names coming into the forward pack.

Cleopas Kundiona retains his place in the front row while milestone man Coles joins Prowse in the second row against Tigers.

Josh Kemeny, with the 27-year-old continues at blindside flanker while Tom Pearson is set to make his first Prem appearance of the season.

Parling has made five changes from the side that endured a 41-17 defeat to Pau.

Solomone Kata returns from injury to start at inside centre, with Gabriel Hamer-Webb and Jack van Poortvliet also coming into the backline to replace Ollie Hassell-Collins and Tom Whiteley respectively.

Aaron Wainwright comes back into the starting lineup in the back row, with Finn Carnduff moving to openside flanker, with Olly Cracknell going at No 8.

Replacements:  R Asiata, T Haffar, W Hurd, J Thompson, J Moro, T Whiteley, O Bailey, G Pearson.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the newly introduced campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

Tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back quickly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” said Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”.

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”.

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

Kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.

#106210. Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (871 w)

Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).
  • Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.
  • In a recent development, by comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).

Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.

In a recent development, by comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea, like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China, where the championships are being held.

In a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.

Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd.".

"Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag.".

Marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, noted that Russian athletes were among the 10 most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.

Sources indicate that "Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an crucial factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka said. "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity.".

Koehler, though, is unconvinced.

Sources indicate that "You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he noted. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system.".

The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.

Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA, the global anti-doping watchdog.

The scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA, Russia's anti-doping agency, has remained suspended for most of the past decade.

As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody.".

WADA noted it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation.".

It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.

Recent findings suggest that "Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place.".

Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.

"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," said Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.

Sources indicate that "There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been.".

Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.

Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.

Nawrocka stated the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.

In April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the agency's head, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.

Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics.".

WADA confirmed to DW only that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Darren Plant | 25 Nov 2026 10:10.
  • Southampton and Middlesbrough square off at St Mary's on Friday night in their first showdown since the conclusion of the Spygate saga.
  • While the visitors sit at the top of the Championship table, the Saints are just seven points adrift of opponents who are now viewed as one of their fierce rivals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 25 Nov 2026 10:10.

Southampton and Middlesbrough square off at St Mary's on Friday night in their first showdown since the conclusion of the Spygate saga.

While the visitors sit at the top of the Championship table, the Saints are just seven points adrift of opponents who are now viewed as one of their fierce rivals.

More than six months on from Tonda Eckert being found guilty of launching a spying mission on a Middlesbrough training session ahead of their playoff semi-final, Southampton have moved on from the controversy that rocked English football.

While Eckert will accept the attention that Friday's game attracts, he will remain focused on trying to secure promotion to the Premier League.

Despite being docked four points as part of their punishment from the Football Association, Southampton can move to within four points of Boro with victory on the South coast.

That said, the Saints have struggled for consistency of late, only collecting five points from four games and conceding a late equaliser to draw 1-1 at Sheffield United on Tuesday night.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, Southampton have been sensational at their home ground. Not only have 22 points being accumulated from a possible 24, they have scored 22 goals and conceded just five.

As for Middlesbrough, they make the long trip south having collected 12 points from eight fixtures, albeit only prevailing on three occasions.

Eight goals had been scored in back-to-back away successes at Stoke City and Bolton Wanderers, yet Kim Hellberg's side have failed to score in the last two such contests versus Wrexham and Watford.

However, 2-0 and 2-1 successes over Bristol City and Swansea City at the Riverside Stadium have ensured that Boro enter this game in top spot with 34 goals from their 17 matches.

It has been revealed that will Lankshear's return from a minor injury may also prove key. Despite being limited to a 62-minute outing versus Swansea, he netted his 14th Championship goal of the season.

Middlesbrough Championship form:.

Eckert will recall a number of his Southampton regulars for this contest, with Jack Stephens, Ryan Manning and Finn Azaz among those who will start.

James Bree may also feature on the back of his 30-minute outing versus Sheffield United after a minor injury, but Leo Scienza is likely to be named on the substitutes' bench at best after missing the last two matches.

Centre-back Keven Schlotterbeck will be sidelined until December through injury.

As for Boro, Sebastian Berhalter is expected to return in central midfield, with Myles Peart-Harris potentially being used further forward.

Providing that Lankshear demonstrates no ill-effects from Tuesday's game, he should start, with David Strelec likely dropping down to the bench to accommodate an extra midfielder.

Despite concerns over an ankle injury, Neto Borges came through 90 minutes versus Swansea and seems in line to be selected at left-back.

Southampton possible starting lineup:.

Peretz; Roerslav, Abbott, Stephens, Manning; Downes, Ward-Prowse; Matsuki, Azaz, Dobbin; Larin.

Middlesbrough possible starting lineup:.

Vitek; Brittain, Phillips, Malanda, Borges; Morris, Berhalter; Cozier-Duberry, Peart-Harris, McGree; Lankshear.

  • Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.
  • It has been revealed that the pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European shares fell sharply in early trading on Friday as a global sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.

Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.

It has been revealed that the pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week. Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines.

European markets had previously weathered the week's turbulence better than their Asian and US counterparts because of their more limited exposure to AI stocks.

Earlier, Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled after a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.5% in early trade, while Seoul's tech-heavy Kospi index slid as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes. Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index was also down more than 8%.

Asian tech giants including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Organization (TSMC) have borne the brunt of the artificial intelligence-related selloff.

Samsung plunged nearly 10% while SK Hynix slid over 11%.

Chip-related shares in Japan also took a beating, with Tokyo Electron stock trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US markets were hammered on Thursday by a sharp retreat in tech stocks, particularly those involved in the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure like data centers.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.52% and shed as much as $2.5 trillion (roughly €2.23 trillion) in market value, while the broader S&P 500 index plunged 4.4%.

The rout occurred as investors grow increasingly anxious about the colossal AI spending plans and whether they will eventually produce commensurate profits.

The results of the US midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both houses of US Congress, added to the concerns.

A number of Democratic governors-elect campaigned on slowing artificial intelligence development and promised to stop or pause the construction of data centers amid growing public opposition to such projects.

"It's pretty clear there's been a real shift ​in sentiment," Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and Upcoming Zealand at online brokerage Moomoo, told the Reuters news agency.

It has been revealed that "Market turning points are often accompanied by strong disagreement, and that indicates up in the market ​by huge swings in either direction," he said. "That's what we appear to have had — and last night's emphatic sell-down suggests that is the direction that we're now headed in.".

By Ben Knapton | 25 Nov 2026 11:33.

Former Leeds United striker Brian Deane, speaking exclusively to Sports Mole, has played down the Whites' chances of signing Will Lankshear in the January transfer window.

The former Tottenham Hotspur youngster has taken the Championship by storm since moving to the Riverside Stadium in the summer, scoring 14 goals in 15 second-tier appearances.

Lankshear netted the winner as Middlesbrough beat Swansea City 2-1 on Tuesday night, a result that saw Kim Hellberg's men move one point clear of Wolverhampton Wanderers at the top of the Championship table.

The 21-year-old unsurprisingly sits top of the Championship top scorers charts, three clear of closest challenger Andri Gudjohnsen of Blackburn Rovers in the race for the Golden Boot.

Lankshear's form has inevitably led to speculation surrounding a swift return to the Premier League, with multiple clubs believed to be interested in securing his services, including Leeds.

Former club Tottenham, Arsenal, Brighton & Hove Albion and Newcastle United have also been credited with an interest, although Middlesbrough's £70m asking price could deter suitors.

Now, former Leeds forward Deane - who scored 44 goals in 199 matches for the Whites - has expressed his view that Lankshear should remain at the Riverside Stadium over the winter.

Industry observers note that “This is his breakout season, and he is at a good club," Deane told Sports Mole. "Middlesbrough look on course to challenge for promotion, so hopefully he gets there with them.

“He will be ambitious and attract attention from clubs such as Leeds, Brighton and Newcastle. He would be a good addition to a squad. But for his own development, I think he is in a good place at Middlesbrough.”.

Lankshear made just six senior appearances for Tottenham before being sold in a £9.8m deal over the summer, and the striker's contract with Middlesbrough does not expire until 2031.

A young striker scoring for fun in the Championship will always attract glances from top-tier clubs, but Lankshear may struggle to force his way into Daniel Farke's first XI right now.

First-choice pairing Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Noah Okafor boast a respectable nine Premier League goals between them in 2026-27, and as long as both are fit, they will spearhead Farke's 3-5-2 system.

Calvert-Lewin is now in the final 24 months of his contract at Elland Road, but the England international is understood to be close to signing a latest Leeds deal.

Lukas Nmecha also provides a steady backup option, although he is due to become a free agent in 2027 and may seek a move away in January if his game-time situation does not improve.

However, Nmecha's proposed exit would then open the door for summer signing Jean-Matteo Bahoya to earn more opportunities, so a winter move for Lankshear would make little sense for all involved.

Brian Deane was speaking to Sports Mole on behalf of BetWright.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Chief executive David Hopkinson, sporting director Ross Wilson, chief financial officer Simon Capper and chief operating officer Brad Miller were on stage discussing head coach Matthias Jaissle, transfers and the prospect of a latest stadium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 07:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 10:59 EST, 24 November 2026.

Newcastle United’s hierarchy addressed supporters at a ‘United We Stand’ event in the shadow of St James’ Park this week.

Chief executive David Hopkinson, sporting director Ross Wilson, chief financial officer Simon Capper and chief operating officer Brad Miller were on stage discussing head coach Matthias Jaissle, transfers and the prospect of a latest stadium.

Our chief football reporter, Craig Hope, was also in the room, and here is his rundown of all the key topics….

‘Arsenal (2-2 draw) felt like a real step forward in the second-half, you felt the energy change in the stadium. But as positive as it was, the biggest feeling we have right now is one of frustration, because the first half wasn't good.

‘We have seen that a few times already this season. An outstanding first half against Hull and a difficult second half. Maybe at Tottenham, 90 minutes straight, really good. Crystal Palace, the second-half very good, first half not.

According to recent reports, ‘So we're definitely trying to find consistency and Saturday was positive. The team felt like they owed that performance to the fans in the second-half. The frustration is that we didn't see that for 90 minutes.’.

Sporting director Ross Wilson and chief executive David Hopkinson were among the members of the Newcastle hierarchy to answer questions from fans on Monday.

The discussion came in the wake of a promising Saturday performance against Arsenal.

HOPE: It would have been easy for Wilson to say, ‘Wasn’t Saturday great? We build from here’. Instead, he gave an honest assessment of where the team is at - because progress cannot really be achieved by playing well for 45 minutes here and there. It felt like a little warning shot, and a fair one.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I want to be really clear (about Vision 2030). I think sometimes it has been misreported as, “Oh, I’m guaranteeing we're going to win by 2030”. No, what I have is guaranteed is that we're in the conversation.

‘(Re 2.0) We set up with a strategy that was very coherent of what we wanted to accomplish this summer. Not incremental change, but necessary and significant change. We lost three players who were important contributors to the past season.

According to recent reports, ‘We set out on a direction under Ross' leadership where we would have a different set of expectations that recognised financial reality. We articulated a vision for the squad here that would be organised around some young talent, who we expect to grow here.

Sources indicate that ‘So I’m delighted with the job Ross did. We executed that strategy superbly. Not everything that we set out to do was accomplished. We went hard on Johan Manzambi and didn't succeed. We went hard on Victor Munoz, didn't succeed, despite thinking we were going to land both of those at one point. But also had successes that we had not anticipated.’.

Sources indicate that HOPE: Wilson also spoke about the strategy of bringing down the squad’s average age, and there appeared to be no panic or concern over the so-far indifferent impact of summer additions. It has been noted by many that on Saturday, in the second half, no upcoming signings were involved apart from goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek. For me, you cannot judge players over three months (look at Lewis Hall) but the substantial price tags attached to some of the young arrivals has raised expectation. Jaissle and the hierarchy need the likes of Matias Fernandez-Pardo, in particular, to start impacting, if questions over summer business are to quieten.

Industry observers note that ’In simple terms, the club had maxed out its credit card in the first few years under the new ownership. We had complied with PSR but it had been incredibly tight, and that forced us to sell at an undervalued price people like Elliot Anderson. We didn’t want to and we didn't want to be there again.

‘So we had to do something differently. The good news is that the Premier League has changed their rules so that there's a bit more headroom now. We’re comfortably within those and we're also comfortably within what we've agreed with UEFA (Newcastle were fined earlier this year). So we're in a really good place. That's the work that David and Ross had talked about in terms of 2.0.

‘That allows us to actually continue to invest and trade. It means that we've got no imperative to sell somebody in January. And it gives us the ability, depending on where we are in the league at the end of this season, to invest again at a proportionate level, depending on what European competition you qualify for.’.

HOPE: The message was clear - there is scope to spend in January and next summer. Newcastle should use that to target goals in the New Year.

Newly introduced Magpies coach Mathias Jaissle was also under the microscope in the shadow of St James' Park.

‘Eddie Howe was a workaholic and he put his heart and soul into the job. So we needed someone who would work hard and the players would not notice a drop off. Matthias works incredibly hard.

‘Eddie was also outstanding on the grass, an elite coach. Again, our players couldn't feel, “Eddie’s gone and they've got another guy who doesn't coach”. Matthias is an expert, elite coach.

‘From a transfer perspective, the head coach at Newcastle always has the final say in any player who comes in. Matthias puts a lot of effort into that - convincing players and making sure they're the right character fit for him. He’s thrown himself into all things Newcastle and we enjoy working with him a lot.’.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Matthias is a clear winner. And you know winners, they win over time. I have a high, high conviction we're going to win under his leadership. I don't think I've ever had the conviction more that we're going to win together than I do right now.’.

HOPE: It is a bold statement from Hopkinson on the back of one win in seven, but the support for Jaissle is clear. He will (and should) be given time, despite an inconsistent start that has included a couple of horror highlights. It was also interesting to note Wilson’s reference to Jaissle’s heavy involvement in transfers, on the back of a week in which the head coach let it be known he wanted more control over transfers.

‘This decision is going to last forever. It will outlast our lifetime. It’s that enormity that means we are taking a little bit of time now.

Industry observers note that ‘Is it going to allow us to compete with the top clubs? Are we going to be able to do it from a financial perspective? Is it going to be transformative for all of our fans, the city and for the region? For all of those reasons, we are very purposely taking our time. But whether we stay at St James’ Park or move, it will be absolutely fantastic.’.

Newcastle continue to mull key decisions on the renovation of their stadium in a bid to unlock upcoming revenue for the club.

Recent findings suggest that ‘We need it (larger stadium) for the revenue a newly introduced stadium will unlock. This is a generational decision and will define the next era of this club. It’s going to be really expensive. We’re advancing significantly into clearly defined options. This is a project with global significance.

According to recent reports, ‘We've spent a lot of time with Fresh York bankers recently thinking through how we might do this and what options we can consider. I can assure you we're working on this every day. I hope we will have something concrete to share with you soon.’.

Industry observers note that HOPE: There was ‘no update’ but the subtext of the discussion was very definitely geared towards a new stadium. I understand this is the direction of travel now, and Hopkinson confirming our story from last week about the high-level talks with Goldman Sachs over how to finance a new stadium demonstrates how advanced the project is.

Industry observers note that overall, the tone of the night was one of ‘we have a plan, stick with us’. It was very different 12 months ago, when the mood in the room was one of huge optimism and excitement at the unveiling of a newly introduced executive team ahead of a Champions League campaign.

Now, it feels like all involved - supporters and those on the inside - realise that this part of the journey will not be easy. That was reflected in the message conveyed.

Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.
  • Recent findings suggest that the question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.
  • Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

Recent findings suggest that the question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care. In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

Recent findings suggest that the 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

In a recent development, the trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, stated Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a fresh cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Industry observers note that eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

Recent findings suggest that in another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell noted that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

It has been revealed that nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

Recent findings suggest that he is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

According to recent reports, in a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

Recent findings suggest that "There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," stated Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together.".

Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

In a recent development, one recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she stated.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and manufacturer. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he stated.
